01: Old rivals the Pennsylvania Railroad and the New York Central merge as Penn Central. It filed for bankruptcy in June 1970, the largest U.S. corporate failure up to that time.
Space Shuttle Columbia breaks apart over Texas and Louisiana during re-entry, its left wing damaged by foam at launch. All seven astronauts are lost.
02: Punxsutawney, Pennsylvania, holds its first formal Groundhog Day. Studies since put the groundhog's forecasts at 35 to 41 percent correct.
Grand Central Terminal opens in New York City, built by and named for the New York Central Railroad.
03: A U-boat torpedoes the troopship Dorchester off Newfoundland. Four Army chaplains give their life jackets to others and go down with the ship; 674 men die.
04: Charles Lindbergh is born in Detroit. In 1927, backed by St. Louis businessmen, he flew the Spirit of St. Louis alone from New York to Paris in just over 33 hours.
05: The BBC broadcasts the Greenwich Time Signal for the first time: six short pips counting up to the hour. They have gone out daily ever since.
06: Jack Kilby of Texas Instruments files for a patent on 'Miniaturized electronic circuits': the integrated circuit. It earned him a Nobel Prize in 2000.
On the Moon with Apollo 14, Alan Shepard hits two golf balls with a six-iron head fixed to a sampling tool. The second, he says, went 'miles and miles and miles.'
07: John Deere is born in Rutland, Vermont. A blacksmith, he made his first polished steel plow at Grand Detour, Illinois, to cut the sticky prairie soil that clogged iron plows.
Bruce McCandless leaves Space Shuttle Challenger with a jet backpack and no safety line, flying about 320 feet from the ship: the first untethered spacewalk.
08: The Nasdaq opens as the world's first electronic stock market: no trading floor, just price quotes on computer screens.
09: President Grant signs the resolution creating a national weather service, placed in the Army Signal Service's Division of Telegrams and Reports for the Benefit of Commerce.
10: RCA Victor presents Glenn Miller with the first gold record, for 1,200,000 copies of 'Chattanooga Choo Choo.'
In Philadelphia, IBM's Deep Blue wins a game against world chess champion Garry Kasparov, a first for a computer under tournament conditions. Kasparov won the match 4-2.
11: Thomas Edison is born in Milan, Ohio. He learned telegraphy as a boy selling papers on the trains out of Port Huron, and worked nights as a railroad telegrapher.
12: Six cars from four nations leave Times Square in the New York to Paris Race. The American Thomas Flyer, driven by George Schuster, reached Paris on July 30 and won.
13: Warsaw, Missouri, records 40 degrees below zero, still the coldest temperature measured in the state. Warsaw also holds Missouri's record high: 118 F in 1954.
14: Lawyers for Alexander Graham Bell and Elisha Gray both file telephone papers at the U.S. Patent Office on the same day. Bell got the patent, No. 174,465, three weeks later.
ENIAC is announced to the public: 18,000 vacuum tubes, more than 30 tons. In a demonstration it works out a missile's trajectory in 15 seconds. The press calls it a 'Giant Brain.'
15: Auguste Chouteau and 30 men begin building at the site Pierre Laclede chose on the west bank of the Mississippi: the founding of St. Louis.
Cyrus McCormick is born in Virginia. He patented his mechanical reaper in 1834; his company became part of International Harvester in 1902.
The battleship USS Maine explodes in Havana harbor, killing 261 of her crew. 'Remember the Maine!' becomes the cry for war with Spain.
16: The nation's first 911 emergency telephone system goes into service in Haleyville, Alabama.
CBBS, the first computer bulletin board system, goes online in Chicago. Ward Christensen and Randy Suess started it while snowed in by the Great Blizzard of 1978.
17: Off Charleston, the Confederate submarine H.L. Hunley sinks USS Housatonic: the first submarine to sink a warship. The Hunley and her eight men never returned.
Volkswagen builds Beetle number 15,007,034, passing the Ford Model T as the most-produced car in history.
18: Elm Farm Ollie, a Guernsey from Bismarck, Missouri, becomes the first cow to fly and be milked in flight, aboard a Ford Trimotor. The milk is parachuted down over St. Louis.
At Lowell Observatory in Arizona, Clyde Tombaugh, 23 and raised on a Kansas farm, discovers Pluto by comparing photographs of the sky taken days apart.
19: U.S. Marines land on Iwo Jima. The battle lasted five weeks and cost about 6,800 American lives.
20: John Glenn orbits the Earth three times in Friendship 7, the first American to do so. His Mercury capsule was built by McDonnell Aircraft in St. Louis.
21: In Wales, Richard Trevithick's steam locomotive hauls 10 tons of iron and 70 men nearly ten miles from Penydarren: the world's first locomotive-hauled railway journey.
The first telephone directory is issued in New Haven, Connecticut: one sheet of cardboard with 50 names and no numbers.
22: The first Daytona 500 ends in a photo finish. Three days later, after studying photographs and newsreels, NASCAR declares Lee Petty the winner over Johnny Beauchamp.
23: President Coolidge signs the Radio Act of 1927, creating the Federal Radio Commission to license broadcasters, hams and ship stations. The FCC replaced it in 1934.
Marines raise the U.S. flag on Mount Suribachi, Iwo Jima. Joe Rosenthal's photograph of the second raising that day won the Pulitzer Prize.
24: Steve Jobs, co-founder of Apple, is born in San Francisco.
25: USS Ranger is launched at Newport News, Virginia, christened by First Lady Lou Henry Hoover: the first U.S. ship designed and built from the keel up as an aircraft carrier.
26: At Daventry, England, Robert Watson-Watt and Arnold Wilkins detect a bomber by radio waves reflected from a BBC shortwave transmitter: the experiment that launched British radar.
27: In the Battle of the Java Sea, a Japanese force defeats an Allied squadron under Dutch Rear Adm. Karel Doorman, who is lost with his flagship De Ruyter.
28: Maryland charters the Baltimore and Ohio Rail Road, which became the first steam-operated common-carrier railroad in the United States.
29: Stranded on Jamaica, Columbus uses an almanac's prediction of that evening's lunar eclipse to frighten the islanders into feeding his crew again.
